I give this game a 10/10. Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number takes place before and in 1991 in Miami. In this game, there are multiple protagonists, all of which have different levels, objectives, and playstyles. The levels are greatly improved from the first. There is way more detail in the levels, sprites and weapons. There are many more enemy types than the first game adding more variety. Most weapons and characters make another appearance as well as some new additions. The gameplay is about the same as the original, kill everyone in the level to leave. Like in the first, you die in 1 shot (2 if you're lucky) and have a wide array of guns and melee weapons. I would only recommend this game to anyone who liked the first because of the story being very well connected to it's predecessor. This game has some of the best music in any video game I have ever played. Also, this game is way more brutal with more gore and ways to kill. In summary, this is how to do a video game sequel. If you buy the first you'll want this too.

The story is brilliant if you like your narrative and the soundtrack is perfect and half the reason I fell in love with this game, if it isn't killing your eardrums you aren't playing it correctly. The level creator just adds more replayability to this game on top of your desire to most likely get better if you don't quit after your first playthrough. All in all it's a brilliant game 10/10 would throw my computer against a wall again

Hmmmm... It's hard for me to accurately give my opinions on this one. I feel like I had more fun with this one than the first, but it also feels like less of a tight, no nonsense experience like the first one. Lots of moments of shoddy map design, and a weird story with an (in my opinion) disappointing end. Without delving too far into spoilers, I enjoyed the various "gimmicks" for characters, like the Ice Climbers character or the pacifist. And by far the greatest thing about this game is the OST. This game is like MGR or Guilty Gear Strive where it's like "how nice of this album to come with a game as well." So I guess overall it's very polarizing, I think it's fantastic but also lackluster at the same time. Definitely worth a play if you liked the first and/or want lots of new jams to add to your workout playlist.

I bought this game after I beat Hotline Miami because I thought it would be as good as the first. Was it? No.
What I experienced instead, was a game with wonky controls, iffy enemy ai, spinning dogs (practically a whole issue by itself)
infuriating obese people and a ''compelling'' storyline that M. Night Shyamalan would tilt his head at. I'm actually kinda sad about it too, all the good nostalgic memories I had with HM are replaced with flashbacks of levels that make me want to punch a hole through my computer screen. And when I thought that maybe Dennaton will make another game that will improve upon the failures of this one, they take the easy way out and with the "everyone fucking dies lmao'' route that doesn't seem out of place in a DnD game. I tried to convince myself that it was good, but there's so much adversity someone can face before they throw in the towel.

4/10. Final thoughts: Disappointed.

Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number follows up on the first Hotline Miami with unique, non-linear story-telling, multiple playable characters, different abilities, and a few more secrets to find. It is a step harder in difficulty, introducing a few new enemies with different ways to approach them. It's always fun, if not frustratingly hard, to do attempts at achieving the highest combo count in all the levels.

For myself, personally, Hotline Miami 2 would have been much shorter if it were not for the introduction of workshop support, allowing for easy access to custom-made levels. I would say that the custom content are half of this game, and the levels and campaigns fans make tend to vary from serious and challenging, to lighthearted and comedic.

Hotline Miami 2 deserves its price point, offering a new challenge to both fans of the previous game, and to players looking for something teeth-grinding to play. And if you hate yourself even more, the game gives you a Hard Mode option at the end of the main campaign. The custom content available both in the workshop and even outside of Steam can really extend replayability, as I still find myself playing through custom levels every now and then.
